paragraphs: He was out of breath.
“Mitya! Mitya!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch hysterically, squeezing out a tear. “Is your father’s blessing nothing to you? What if I curse you?”
“Shameless hypocrite!” Dmitri exclaimed furiously.

“That’s what he says to his father! His father! What would he say to other people? Gentlemen, just imagine: there’s a poor but honorable man living here, weighed down with a large family, a captain who got into trouble and was dismissed from the army, but not publicly, not by court-martial, with no stain on his honor. And three weeks ago Dmitri seized him by the beard in a tavern, dragged him out into the street and beat him in public, and all because he acts as an agent for me in a little business of mine.”

“It’s all a lie! On the surface it’s true, but underneath it’s a lie!” Dmitri was shaking with rage. “Father, I don’t defend what I did. Yes, I admit it openly: I behaved like a brute to that captain, and I regret it now, and I’m disgusted with myself for my brutal rage. But this captain, this agent of yours, went to that lady whom you call an enchantress. He proposed to her, on your behalf, that she should take the I.O.U.’s of mine that you hold and sue me for the money, to put me in prison with them, if I kept on demanding an account from you of my property. Now you reproach me for having a weakness for that lady, when you yourself egged her on to captivate me! She told me so to my face.... She told me the story and laughed at you.... You wanted to put me in prison because you’re jealous of me over her, because you’d begun to force your attentions on her. I know all about that, too. She laughed at you for that as well—you hear?—she laughed at you as she told it. So here you have this man, this father, who reproaches his dissolute son! Gentlemen, forgive my anger, but I knew this crafty old man would only bring you together to make a scandal. I had come to forgive him if he held out his hand. To forgive him, and to ask his forgiveness! But he has just this minute insulted not only me but an honorable young lady, for whom I feel such reverence that I dare not take her name in vain. So I’ve made up my mind to expose his game, though he is my father....”

He could not go on. His eyes were glittering and he breathed with difficulty. But everyone in the cell was stirred. Everyone except Father Zossima rose uneasily from their seats. The monks looked stern, but they waited for a sign from the elder. He sat still, pale, not from excitement but from the weakness of his illness. An imploring smile lit up his face. From time to time he raised his hand as though to hold back the storm, and of course a gesture from him would have been enough to end the scene. But he seemed to be waiting for something, and watched them intently, as though trying to make out something that was not quite clear to him. At last Miüsov felt completely humiliated and disgraced.

“We are all to blame for this disgraceful scene,” he said hotly. “But I did not foresee it when I came, though I knew whom I was dealing with. This must be stopped at once! Believe me, your reverence, I had no exact knowledge of the details that have just come to light. I was unwilling to believe them, and I am learning them for the first time.... A father is jealous of his son’s relations with a woman of loose behavior, and plots with the creature to get his son put in prison! This is the company I’ve been forced to sit in! I was deceived. I tell you all that I was as much deceived as anyone.”

“Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly yelled, in an unnatural voice, “if you weren’t my son, I would challenge you this instant to a duel ... with pistols, at three paces ... across a handkerchief,” he finished, stamping with both feet.

Old liars who have been acting all their lives sometimes get so completely caught up in their part that they tremble or weep real tears of feeling, even though at that very moment, or a second later, they can whisper to themselves, “You know you’re lying, you shameless old sinner! You’re acting now, in spite of your ‘holy’ wrath.”
Dmitri frowned painfully and looked at his father with unspeakable contempt.

“I thought ... I thought,” he said in a soft and, as it were, controlled voice, “that I was coming back to my native place with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to look after him in his old age. And I find nothing but a depraved libertine, a despicable clown!”

“A duel!” the old wretch yelled again, breathless, spluttering over every syllable. “And you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, let me tell you that there has never been in all your family a loftier and more honest—you hear—more honest woman than this ‘creature,’ as you have dared to call her! And you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, have abandoned your betrothed for that ‘creature,’ so you must have thought yourself that your betrothed couldn’t hold a candle to her. That’s the woman you call a ‘creature’!”
“Shameful!” broke from Father Iosif.
“Shameful and disgraceful!” cried Kalganov in a boyish voice, flushing crimson and trembling with emotion. He had been silent until that moment.

“Why is such a man alive?” Dmitri growled in a hollow voice, beside himself with rage, hunching up his shoulders until he looked almost deformed. “Tell me, can he be allowed to go on defiling the earth?” He looked around at everyone and pointed at the old man. He spoke evenly and deliberately.

“Listen, listen, monks, to the parricide!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, rushing up to Father Iosif. “That’s the answer to your ‘shameful!’ What is shameful? That ‘creature,’ that ‘woman of loose behavior,’ is perhaps holier than you are yourselves, you monks who are seeking salvation! She fell, perhaps, in her youth, ruined by her surroundings. But she loved much, and Christ himself forgave the woman ‘who loved much.’”
“It was not for such love that Christ forgave her,” broke in the gentle Father Iosif impatiently.
“Yes, it was for such love, monks, it was! You save your souls here, eating cabbage, and think you are the righteous. You eat one little fish a day, and you think you can bribe God with a fish.”
“This is unbearable!” was heard on all sides in the cell.

But this disgraceful scene was cut short in a most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Alyosha was almost beside himself with worry for the elder and for everyone else, but he managed to support him by the arm. Father Zossima moved toward Dmitri, and when he reached him he sank to his knees before him. Alyosha thought he had fallen from weakness, but it was not so. The elder deliberately bowed down at Dmitri’s feet, clearly and fully, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so astounded that he failed to help him when he got up again. There was a faint smile on his lips.
“Good-by! Forgive me, all of you!” he said, bowing to his guests on every side.

Dmitri stood for a few moments in amazement. Bowing down to him—what did it mean? Suddenly he cried aloud, “Oh, God!” hid his face in his hands and rushed out of the room. All the guests flocked out after him, in their confusion not saying good-by or bowing to their host. Only the monks went up to him again for a blessing.

“What did it mean, falling at his feet like that? Was it symbolic, or what?” said Fyodor Pavlovitch, suddenly quiet, trying to start up a conversation again without daring to speak to anyone in particular. They were all just then leaving the grounds of the hermitage.
“I can’t answer for a madhouse and for madmen,” Miüsov answered at once, in ill humor. “But I will spare myself your company, Fyodor Pavlovitch, and, believe me, for ever. Where’s that monk?”

“That monk,” that is, the monk who had invited them to dine with the Superior, did not keep them waiting. He met them as soon as they came down the steps from the elder’s cell, as though he had been waiting for them all along.

“Reverend Father, please do me a favor. Give my deepest respects to the Father Superior, and apologize for me, Miüsov, personally to his reverence. Tell him I deeply regret that, because of unforeseen circumstances, I cannot have the honor of being at his table, much as I would like to,” Miüsov said irritably to the monk.

“And that unforeseen circumstance, of course, is me,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut in at once. “Do you hear, Father? This gentleman doesn’t want to stay in my company, or else he’d go right away. And you shall go, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, please go to the Father Superior, and good appetite to you. I’ll be the one to decline, not you. Home, home, I’ll eat at home. I don’t feel up to it here, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, my amiable relative.”
“I am not your relative and never have been, you contemptible man!”

“I said it on purpose to madden you, because you always deny the relationship, though you really are a relation, in spite of all your squirming. I’ll prove it from the church calendar. As for you, Ivan, stay if you like. I’ll send the horses for you later. Good manners require you to go to the Father Superior, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to apologize for the disturbance we’ve been making....”
“Is it true that you’re going home? You aren’t lying?”

“Pyotr Alexandrovitch! How could I dare, after what’s happened! Forgive me, gentlemen, I was carried away! And upset, too! And, really, I am ashamed. Gentlemen, one man has the heart of Alexander of Macedon and another the heart of the little dog Fido. Mine is the heart of the little dog Fido. I am ashamed! After such an escapade, how can I go to dinner and gobble up the monastery’s sauces? I am ashamed, I can’t. You must excuse me!”

“The devil only knows, what if he’s deceiving us?” thought Miüsov, still hesitating, and he watched the retreating buffoon with distrustful eyes. The buffoon turned around, and seeing that Miüsov was watching him, blew him a kiss.
“Well, are you coming to the Superior’s?” Miüsov asked Ivan abruptly.
“Why not? I was specially invited yesterday.”

“Unfortunately I feel obliged to go to this confounded dinner,” said Miüsov, with the same irritability, not caring that the monk was listening. “We ought at least to apologize for the disturbance and explain that it wasn’t our doing. What do you think?”
“Yes, we must explain that it wasn’t our doing. Besides, Father won’t be there,” Ivan remarked.
“Well, I should hope not! Confound this dinner!”

They all walked on, however. The monk listened in silence. On the road through the copse he made one remark—that the Father Superior had been waiting a long time, and that they were more than half an hour late. He got no answer. Miüsov looked at Ivan with hatred.
“Look at him, going to the dinner as though nothing had happened,” he thought. “A brazen face, and the conscience of a Karamazov!”
